knowledge_point.title: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent

question.:question/worked-solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $100{x}^{2}=(10x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=10x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{10}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+100{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(10x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{10}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(10x)}{10}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $10{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{10}x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{10}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{10}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+10{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(\sqrt{10}x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{10}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{81+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{81\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/81)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{81}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/81}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{81}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/9)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{9})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{9}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{9}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=9\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{81+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{81}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/9)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{81}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (9\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{9})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{36\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/36)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{36}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/36}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{36}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/6)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}.$ 

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{6}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=6\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{36}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/6)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{36}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (6\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{6})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{7}{6+96{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{7}{6}\int\frac{1}{1+16{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int\frac{1}{1+u^2}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $16x^2=(4x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{6+96{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x&=\frac{7}{6}\int\frac{1}{1+(4x)^2}\,\text{d}x\\&=\frac{7}{6}\int\frac{1}{1+u^2}\cdot\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u\\&=\frac{7}{24}\int\frac{1}{1+u^2}\,\text{d}u\\&=\frac{7}{24}\operatorname{arctan}u+C\\&=\frac{7}{24}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(4x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{5}{7+252{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{5}{7}\int\frac{1}{1+36{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int\frac{1}{1+u^2}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $36x^2=(6x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=6x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{7+252{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x&=\frac{5}{7}\int\frac{1}{1+(6x)^2}\,\text{d}x\\&=\frac{5}{7}\int\frac{1}{1+u^2}\cdot\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u\\&=\frac{5}{42}\int\frac{1}{1+u^2}\,\text{d}u\\&=\frac{5}{42}\operatorname{arctan}u+C\\&=\frac{5}{42}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(6x)+C\end{aligned}
$$
